passage:
I'm Jyoti, and Ankita has been my best friend since first year. She's the most talented illustrator in our design batch, and this year she has turned down everything. The college magazine cover: "Not good enough yet." The children's book project with a real publisher: "Maybe next year." The group show: she didn't even reply.
I can't read her mind, but whenever someone praises her old work, she looks almost pained.
Last month I tried something different. I brought my own sketchbook, the messy one, full of crossed-out hands and wonky faces, and showed her page after page. "This is how mine start," I said. She laughed at a horse that looked like a sofa.
Then I stopped saying "your work is amazing" and started saying things like "you tried a new brush today" or "that's further than yesterday."
On Friday she sent me a rough sketch for the magazine. Just a rough one. I didn't make a fuss.

qa.q: What did one of Jyoti's sketches look like, according to Ankita's laugh?
qa.a: A horse that looked like a sofa.

qa.q: Why might Ankita look almost pained when her old work is praised?
qa.a: Praise for results may feel like a standard she must keep meeting, so it adds to her fear of making something less than perfect.

qa.q: Which of Jyoti's changes helped Ankita, and why?
qa.a: Showing Jyoti's own messy sketchbook and praising effort and progress instead of results made imperfect work feel normal and safer to share.

qa.q: What might it have meant for Ankita to see Jyoti's crossed-out hands and wonky faces?
qa.a: It may have shown Ankita that even good artists start messily, easing her belief that only perfect work can be seen.

grounding: Shows a friend who notices a talented illustrator turning down chances, and helps by sharing her own messy sketches and praising effort and progress.

passage:
Monday, first week of term. Dr Deepika Rao noticed that Trisha, the sharpest student in her economics seminar, had not submitted the optional essay again, and had quietly declined the research assistant post Deepika offered. "I'm not ready," Trisha said, eyes down.
Thursday, two weeks later. Deepika tried something she had never done in class. She put her own first draft of a journal paper on the projector, red notes and all, including a paragraph she had rewritten six times. "This is what my work looks like before it's good," she said. The class laughed. Trisha leaned forward.
Friday, a month later. Trisha handed in a messy two-page draft with a note: "Not finished." Deepika wrote back only about what she had tried: "Bold argument in section two. Good progress from your first idea."
The next week Trisha asked whether the assistant post was still open.

qa.q: What did Deepika put on the projector?
qa.a: Her own first draft of a journal paper, red notes and all.

qa.q: What does Trisha's 'I'm not ready', said with eyes down, suggest?
qa.a: It suggests fear of producing less than perfect work rather than a lack of ability.

qa.q: Which of Deepika's responses helped loosen Trisha's grip, and why?
qa.a: Showing her own flawed draft and commenting on effort and progress rather than polish made imperfect work feel safe to hand in.

qa.q: How might Trisha have felt seeing the lecturer's red-marked draft?
qa.a: Trisha may have felt surprised and relieved that even an expert's writing starts rough, which is why she leaned forward.

grounding: Illustrates a lecturer who sees a strong student declining chances, and helps by showing her own messy draft and praising effort and progress.
